s: C. Congressional control of federal jurisdiction.
Article III vests judicial power in "one supreme Court" and "such inferior Courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish."
Article III also gives the Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction "with such Exceptions, and under such Regulations as the Congress shall make."
Under the traditional "Madisonian compromise," Congress could have created no lower federal courts at all, so it may define their jurisdiction narrowly (Sheldon v. Sill, 1850).
Exceptions to Supreme Court appellate jurisdiction.
In Ex parte McCardle (1869), Congress repealed the statute under which a pending habeas appeal had been filed, and the Court dismissed.
It noted, however, that other routes to review remained (Ex parte Yerger).
Scholars debate whether Congress may strip all federal jurisdiction over a constitutional claim (Henry Hart's "essential functions" thesis).
Congress may not use jurisdictional rules to dictate the outcome of a particular case under existing law (United States v. Klein, 1872).
Changing the underlying law and applying it to pending cases is permitted (Bank Markazi v. Peterson, 2016; Patchak v. Zinke, 2018).
Congress may not reopen final judgments (Plaut).
Jurisdictional restrictions may not themselves violate other provisions: equal protection, due process, or the Suspension Clause (Boumediene v. Bush, 2008).

Congress may assign some matters to non-Article III tribunals ("public rights"), but private-rights claims of the kind traditionally tried at common law require an Article III court (Stern v. Marshall, 2011; Oil States, 2018).
When such claims seek civil penalties resembling common-law suits, the Seventh Amendment requires a jury (SEC v. Jarkesy, 2024).
